title: What is Mircoservice?

blocks.content:
Microservices are an architectural style where an application is built as a collection of small, independent, and loosely
coupled services.

title: How do Microservices differ from Monolithic Architecture?

cells.content: The entire application is built and deployed as a single unit.
The application is divided into small, independent services, each responsible for a specific business functionality. Scalability:
The entire application needs to be scaled even if only one feature requires more resources.
Individual services can be scaled independently based on their requirements.
Usually uses a common technology stack across the application.
Different services can use different technologies or programming languages.
A small change may require redeploying the entire application.
Individual services can be deployed independently without redeploying the entire system.
Suitable for small applications, simple systems, or applications where simplicity is important.
Suitable for large, complex applications where independent development, deployment, and scaling of business functionalities are required.

title: what are the key features of microservices?

blocks.content: Key Features of Microservices

items.title: Independent Deployment
items.description: Each microservice can be developed, tested, and deployed independently without redeploying the entire application.

items.title: Fault Isolation
items.description: Failure in one microservice does not necessarily bring down the entire application. Other services can continue to operate independently.

items.title: Scalability
items.description: Individual services can be scaled independently based on their workload or resource requirements.

title: Name the main components of Microservices?

items.title: Service Independence
items.description: Each microservice is independently developed, deployed, and maintained.

items.title: Domain-Driven Design (DDD)
items.description: Services are organized around specific business domains or capabilities.

items.title: API Communication
items.description: Microservices communicate with each other through APIs, commonly REST, gRPC, or messaging.

items.title: Technology Diversity
items.description: Different microservices can use different programming languages, frameworks, or technologies based on their requirements.

items.title: Service Registry and Discovery
items.description: Helps services find and communicate with other available services dynamically.

items.title: API Gateway
items.description: Acts as a single entry point for clients and routes requests to the appropriate microservice.

items.title: Load Balancer
items.description: Distributes incoming requests across multiple instances of a service to improve availability and performance.

items.title: Data Management
items.description: Each service typically manages its own data and database to maintain loose coupling.

items.title: Monitoring and Logging
items.description: Tracks service health, performance, errors, and application activity across the distributed system.

items.title: CI/CD Pipeline
items.description: Automates building, testing, and deploying individual microservices independently.

title: Explain the role of an API Gateway in Microservices?

blocks.content: An API Gateway is the single entry point for clients in a microservices architecture. It handles concerns like request routing, authentication, rate limiting, load balancing, and response aggregation, so clients don't need to communicate directly with individual microservices.

items.title: Request Routing
items.description: Routes client requests to the appropriate microservice.

items.title: Authentication & Authorization
items.description: Validates JWT tokens and controls access to services.

items.title: Load Balancing
items.description: Distributes requests across multiple instances of a service.

items.title: Rate Limiting
items.description: Controls the number of requests to protect services from excessive traffic.

items.title: Response Aggregation
items.description: Can combine responses from multiple microservices into a single response.

items.title: Logging & Monitoring
items.description: Centralizes request logging, tracing, and monitoring.

items.title: Protocol Transformation
items.description: Can translate between protocols such as HTTP and gRPC.

title: What is Service Discovery in Microservices?

blocks.content:
Service Discovery is a mechanism that enables microservices to dynamically locate and communicate with each other within a distributed system. It ensures that services can find and connect to other services without hard-coded
configurations, promoting flexibility and scalability.

items.description: A microservice starts and registers itself with a Service Registry.
The registry stores its service name, IP address, port, and health status.
When another service needs to communicate with it, it queries the registry.
The registry returns an available instance.
The calling service sends the request to that instance.

blocks.code:
Order Service
     |
     | "Where is Payment Service?"
     ↓
Service Registry
     |
     | "Payment Service → 10.0.1.15:5002"
     ↓
Payment Service

blocks.text: Common tools include Consul, Eureka, and Kubernetes Service Discovery.

blocks.content: Service Discovery allows microservices to dynamically locate and communicate with other service instances without hardcoding IP addresses or ports. Services register themselves with a service registry, and other services query the registry to find an available instance.

title: What is a Container, and Why is it Used in Microservices?

blocks.content: A container is a lightweight, standalone unit that bundles an application along with its dependencies, including libraries, configurations and runtime to ensure consistency across different environments.

blocks.text: Why are Containers Used in Microservices?

items.title: Isolation
items.description: Each microservice runs independently in its own container.

items.title: Portability
items.description: The same container can run on a developer machine, server, or cloud environment.

items.title: Scalability
items.description: Multiple instances of a service can be easily created when demand increases.

items.title: Consistent Environment
items.description: Avoids the common "works on my machine" problem.

items.title: Fast Deployment
items.description: Containers are lightweight and can start quickly.

items.title: Independent Deployment
items.description: Each microservice can be built, deployed, updated, and restarted independently.

blocks.code:
API Gateway
                         |
        +----------------+----------------+
        |                |                |
   User Service     Order Service    Payment Service
        |                |                |
   Container 1      Container 2      Container 3

blocks.content: Docker is commonly used to create and run containers, while platforms such as Kubernetes can manage containers at scale.

title: How do Microservices Communicate with each other?

blocks.content: Microservices communicate mainly through synchronous protocols like REST and gRPC, or asynchronously through message brokers like Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ, or Kafka.
We choose synchronous communication when an immediate response is required and asynchronous communication when we want loose coupling and independent processing.

items.title: Synchronous Communication
items.description: One service directly calls another service and waits for a response, usually through REST APIs or gRPC.

items.title: Asynchronous Communication
items.description: A service sends a message/event through a message broker, and the receiving service processes it independently. Common technologies include Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ, and Kafka.

blocks.code:
Synchronous:

Order Service
     |
     | HTTP / REST
     ↓
Payment Service
     |
     ↓
Payment Response

Asynchronous:

Order Service
     |
     | OrderCreated Event
     ↓
Message Broker
     |
     ↓
Payment Service

title: How Would You Handle a Microservice Failure?

blocks.content: I would handle microservice failures using timeouts, retries with exponential backoff, circuit breakers, fallbacks, health checks, and monitoring. For asynchronous communication, I would use a message broker so messages aren't lost during temporary service failures. The goal is to isolate the failure and keep the rest of the system available.

title: How can you ensure backward compatibility in Microservices

blocks.content: I ensure backward compatibility by using API versioning, maintaining existing contracts, making additive rather than breaking changes, and using contract testing. I also use a proper deprecation strategy and ensure database and event-schema changes remain compatible during rolling deployments.
A deprecation strategy is a planned process for retiring an old API or service version without suddenly breaking existing consumers.

title: What is the meaning of OAuth and why is it used?

blocks.content: OAuth(Open Authorization) is an authorization framework that allows users to grant third-party applications limited access to their resources using an access token, without sharing their password. The access token defines what resources the application can access and for how long.

items.title: Secure Authorization
items.description: Gives an application limited access to specific resources.

items.title: No Password Sharing
items.description: The application doesn't need the user's password.

items.title: Access Tokens
items.description: Uses tokens to access protected resources.

items.title: Scoped Access
items.description: Permissions can be restricted, such as read-only access.

items.title: Token Expiration
items.description: Access tokens can have a limited lifetime.

items.title: Third-Party Integration
items.description: Commonly used when applications need to interact with external services.

blocks.content: Suppose you click "Sign in with Google":

blocks.code:
Your App
            |
      Request authorization
            | 
            ↓
         Google
            |
      User grants permission
            | 
            ↓
     Authorization Server
            |
       Access Token
            | 
            ↓
         Your App
            |
            | 
        Access Token
            ↓
         Google API

blocks.content: Your application receives an access token, rather than your Google password, and uses that token to access the resources it has been authorized to access.

items.title: OAuth
items.description: Defines how authorization is granted and how access to resources is delegated.

items.title: JWT
items.description: A token format that can be used to carry claims/identity information.

blocks.content: OAuth and JWT are therefore not alternatives; OAuth can use JWTs as tokens.

title: What is CQRS pattern in microservices? What problem does it solve

blocks.content: CQRS stands for Command Query Responsibility Segregation. It separates read operations from write operations by using different models or services for commands and queries. It solves problems such as high read/write workload differences, scalability, and complex data retrieval by allowing each side to be optimized and scaled independently.
In simple terms:

blocks.code:
Client
                |
           API Gateway
                |
        ┌───────┴───────┐
        ↓               ↓
     Command          Query
     (Write)           (Read)
        ↓               ↓
   Write Database    Read Database

blocks.content: The main problem is that read and write operations often have different requirements.
For example, in an insurance system:

items.title: Command
items.description: Update customer's salary

items.title: Command
items.description: Add a new benefit

items.title: Query
items.description: Get customer policy details

items.title: Query
items.description: Generate a customer wealth report

blocks.content: CQRS does not necessarily mean two separate databases. You can implement CQRS with the same database but separate command/query models, or use separate read and write databases when the architecture requires it.

title: Compare API gateway and load balancer

blocks.content: An API Gateway is the single entry point for clients and handles API-level responsibilities such as request routing, authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and response aggregation. A Load Balancer mainly distributes incoming traffic across multiple healthy instances of the same service to improve availability and scalability.
Simple difference:

blocks.code: Client → API Gateway → Order Service → Load Balancer → Order Instance 1 / 2 / 3

blocks.content: A gateway decides “which service should handle this request?”, while a load balancer decides “which instance of that service should handle it?”

title: What are some common microservices design principles ?

blocks.content: Some common microservices design principles are single responsibility, loose coupling, high cohesion, independent deployment, and decentralized data management. We also follow principles like API-based communication, fault isolation, scalability, observability, and automation through CI/CD.

items.title: Single Responsibility
items.description: Each service handles one business capability.

items.title: Loose Coupling
items.description: Services should depend on contracts rather than internal implementation.

items.title: Independent Deployment
items.description: One service can be deployed without deploying the entire system.

items.title: Fault Isolation
items.description: Failure of one service should not bring down the whole application.

items.title: Decentralized Data
items.description: Each service owns its data rather than sharing one database directly.

items.title: Scalability
items.description: Scale individual services based on their workload.

blocks.content: The interviewer mainly wants to hear independence, loose coupling, fault isolation, scalability, and clear service boundaries.

title: How do you ensure security?

blocks.content: In microservices, I ensure security by using HTTPS for communication, OAuth 2.0/JWT for authentication and authorization, and role-based access control for protecting APIs. I also validate inputs, secure secrets using services like Azure Key Vault, apply rate limiting at the API Gateway, and use proper logging and monitoring to detect suspicious activity.
A user authenticates and receives a JWT access token. The API Gateway validates the token, and individual services verify the required roles or permissions before processing the request.

title: What are few ways to achieve synchronous and asynchronous communication between microservices

blocks.content: Microservices can communicate synchronously using REST APIs or gRPC, where the caller waits for an immediate response. For asynchronous communication, we can use message brokers such as Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ, or Kafka, where one service publishes a message or event and another service processes it independently.

items.title: Synchronous
items.code: Order Service → REST API → Payment Service → Response

items.title: Asynchronous
items.code: Order Service → Azure Service Bus → Payment Service

blocks.content: Use synchronous communication when an immediate response is required and asynchronous communication when we want loose coupling, independent processing, and better resilience.

In a food delivery application, once the Order Service successfully creates an order, it can immediately respond with ‘Order placed successfully’. It can then publish an OrderCreated event to a message broker and downstream services such as notification, restaurant processing and delivery can process that event asynchronously.

blocks.code:
User selects food
      ↓
Place Order
      ↓
Order Service
      ↓
Order created successfully
      ↓
"Order Placed" response to user
      │
      └────→ Message Queue
                ↓
        ┌───────┼────────┐
        ↓       ↓        ↓
     Restaurant  Payment  Notification
     processing  events   service
        ↓
     Delivery assignment
        ↓
     Delivery tracking

title: How do you implement rate limiting?

blocks.content: Rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make to an API within a specific time period. In a microservices architecture, I can implement it at the API Gateway or API level using algorithms like Fixed Window, Sliding Window, or Token Bucket, and return HTTP 429 when the limit is exceeded.
We can allow a user to make 100 requests per minute. If the user exceeds the limit, the API returns 429 Too Many Requests, and the client can retry after the specified time.
Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse, excessive traffic, and overload, while helping maintain availability for other users.

title: What is event driven architecture in microservices?

blocks.content: Event-Driven Architecture is a microservices approach where services communicate through events instead of directly calling each other. When something happens one service publishes an event to a message broker and other interested services consume that event and process it independently.

blocks.code:
Order Service
     ↓
 OrderCreated Event
     ↓
Message Broker (Azure Service Bus)
     ├──→ Payment Service
     ├──→ Notification Service
     └──→ Delivery Service

blocks.content: For example, when an order is created the Order Service publishes an OrderCreated event. Payment, notification and delivery services can consume that event independently.

title: What is idempotency and why is it important in microservices?

blocks.content: Idempotency means performing the same operation multiple times produces the same final result as performing it once. It is important in microservices because network failures, retries or duplicate messages can cause the same request to be processed multiple times potentially creating duplicate transactions.

For example, if a payment request times out, the client may retry it. We can use a unique Idempotency Key for that payment, so even if the request is received multiple times, the payment is processed only once.
Idempotency protects against duplicate processing, especially with retries and asynchronous messaging.

title: What is database sharding and why is it used in microservices

blocks.content: Database sharding is a technique of splitting a large database into smaller, independent partitions called shards, where each shard contains a subset of the data. In microservices, it is used to handle large data volumes and high traffic by distributing data and database load across multiple servers, improving scalability and performance.
An application with millions of customers could shard customer data based on CustomerId, so customers 1–1 million are stored in one shard and the next group in another.
Sharding = horizontal data partitioning used mainly for scalability and reducing database load.

title: How do you handle data consistency in Microservices?

blocks.content: In microservices, I handle data consistency using database transactions within each service and patterns like Saga for maintaining consistency across multiple services. For asynchronous operations, I use events and message brokers, along with retries and idempotency to handle failures and duplicate messages.
In an order process, Order, Payment and Inventory may have separate databases. A Saga coordinates these operations, and if payment fails, a compensating action can cancel or roll back the order.

title: What is canary deployment

blocks.content: Canary deployment is a deployment strategy where we release a new version of an application to a small percentage of users or traffic first, instead of releasing it to everyone at once. We monitor its performance, errors and user impact, and if everything looks good. we gradually increase the traffic to the new version.

blocks.code:
100% Traffic
          ↓
   95% → Old Version
    5% → New Version
           ↓
       Monitor
           ↓
      Everything OK
           ↓
   50% → New Version
           ↓
  100% → New Version

blocks.content: Canary deployment reduces deployment risk by exposing the new version gradually and allowing us to roll back quickly if problems occur.

title: How would you monitor microservices?

blocks.content: I would monitor microservices using centralized logging, metrics, distributed tracing and health checks. I would track metrics such as CPU, memory, request rate, response time, error rate and service availability. while using correlation IDs and distributed tracing to trace a request across multiple services.

In Azure, I could use Application Insights and Azure Monitor to collect application logs, performance metrics, exceptions and distributed traces. Alerts can then notify the team when error rates or response times cross defined thresholds.

title: What are the DDD principles?

blocks.content: DDD stands for Domain-Driven Design. Its main principle is to design the software around the business domain and its business rules rather than focusing only on technical implementation. Key DDD concepts include bounded contexts, entities, value objects, aggregates, repositories, and domain services.

items.title: Ubiquitous Language
items.description: Developers and business use the same terminology.

items.title: Bounded Context
items.description: Clearly defines the boundary of a particular domain.

items.title: Entities
items.description: Objects identified by a unique identity.

items.title: Value Objects
items.description: Objects defined by their values rather than identity.

items.title: Aggregates
items.description: Group related entities/value objects with a single consistency boundary.

items.title: Domain Services
items.description: Business logic that doesn't naturally belong to an entity/value object.

blocks.content: In an insurance system, Policy could be an Entity, Address could be a Value Object and Policy with its related Policy Benefits could form an Aggregate. Different areas such as Claims and Policy Management could be separate Bounded Contexts.

title: How do you design for scalability?

blocks.content: I design for scalability by keeping services stateless, allowing horizontal scaling, using load balancing, caching, asynchronous messaging, and database optimization. I also monitor system performance and scale individual microservices independently based on their workload.
If the Order Service receives high traffic, instead of increasing resources on a single instance, I can run multiple instances behind a load balancer and scale them based on CPU or request volume.
Stateless services + horizontal scaling + load balancing + caching + async processing + database optimization.

title: What is chaos engineering and how is it applied?

blocks.content: Chaos engineering is the practice of intentionally introducing controlled failures into a system to test its resilience and identify weaknesses. In microservices, we can simulate failures such as stopping a service, increasing network latency, or making a dependency unavailable, and then verify that mechanisms like retries, circuit breakers, fallbacks, and monitoring work correctly.

For example, we can intentionally make the Payment Service unavailable in a test environment and verify that the Order Service handles the failure gracefully using a timeout, retry and fallback instead of bringing down the entire application.

title: How do you perform logging in a distributed microservices system?

blocks.content: In a distributed microservices system, I use centralized logging so logs from all services are collected and searchable in one place. I also use a unique correlation ID or trace ID for each request, so I can trace the same request across multiple services and troubleshoot failures easily.

For example, in Azure, I can use Application Insights and Azure Monitor to collect logs and traces from multiple services. If a request passes through Order, Payment and Notification services, the same correlation ID helps me track that request across all three.

title: What is the purpose of a retry pattern?

blocks.content: The Retry Pattern is used to automatically retry a failed operation when the failure is temporary or transient, such as a network issue, temporary service unavailability, or timeout.
Instead of failing immediately, the system retries the request a limited number of times, usually with exponential backoff between attempts.
Suppose Order Service calls Payment Service, but Payment Service temporarily times out:

blocks.code:
Order Service
     ↓
Payment Service → Timeout
     ↓
Retry after 1 sec
     ↓
Payment Service → Timeout
     ↓
Retry after 2 sec
     ↓
Payment Service → Success

blocks.content:
Retry = recover from temporary failures automatically.

In production, combine retries with timeouts and circuit breakers, and avoid retrying non-transient errors such as 400 Bad Request.

title: What are sidecars in microservices?

blocks.content: A Sidecar is a separate process or container that runs alongside a microservice and provides common supporting functionality without putting that functionality directly into the application code.
For example, a sidecar can handle logging, monitoring, security, service-to-service communication, retries, or configuration.

blocks.code:
Order Service Container
        +
Sidecar Container
        ↓
Logging / Monitoring / Security / Communication

blocks.content: In Kubernetes, the application container and sidecar container typically run in the same Pod and can communicate over the local network.

title: What are the best practices for deploying microservices in prod environment?

blocks.content: For deploying microservices in production, I follow practices like containerization, CI/CD automation, independent deployment, health checks, centralized logging and monitoring, secure configuration, and proper scaling.
I also use deployment strategies such as Blue-Green or Canary deployment to reduce downtime and deployment risk, along with load balancing, autoscaling, rollback mechanisms, and secrets management.
For an Order Service:

blocks.code:
Developer → Git → CI/CD Pipeline
                    ↓
              Build & Test
                    ↓
             Docker Image
                    ↓
          Deploy to Kubernetes
                    ↓
       Health Check + Monitoring
                    ↓
       Canary: 5% → 25% → 100%

items.description: consistent deployment

items.title: CI/CD
items.description: automated build, test, deployment

items.title: Health checks
items.description: detect unhealthy instances

items.title: Load balancing
items.description: distribute traffic

items.description: safer releases

items.title: Secrets management

items.title: Centralized logging + monitoring

blocks.content: In production, I focus on automated CI/CD, containerization, security, observability, scalability, health checks, and zero/minimal-downtime deployment with a reliable rollback strategy.
